title: Should You Hold Students Accountable On The Last Day Of School? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/06/03/hold-students-accountable-the-last-day-of-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues emphatically that teachers should continue enforcing their classroom management plan through the very last day of school, even when it seems inconsequential. He frames consistency at these low-stakes moments — the last day, a field trip, a class party — as a defining test of integrity, since abandoning follow-through signals to students that a teacher's promises were never fully sincere. Linsin contends that zero-wiggle-room consistency is actually easier than situational judgment calls, since it removes doubt and decision fatigue, and that this discipline compounds into strength for the following school year. He frames the memory students carry of a teacher's integrity as something that can support them through future moral dilemmas, elevating the final-day decision beyond a matter of classroom order into an act of lasting character education. The piece closes by reframing these easy-to-skip moments as valuable opportunities rather than final formalities.
points: Teachers should continue enforcing the classroom management plan through the very last day of school, not treat it as inconsequential.
Abandoning follow-through at low-stakes moments (last day, parties, field trips) signals to students that a teacher's promises were never fully sincere.
Zero-wiggle-room consistency is described as easier, not harder, than situational judgment calls, since it removes doubt and decision fatigue.
Students carry the memory of a teacher's integrity into future moments of moral difficulty in their own lives.
Maintaining consistency to the final bell strengthens a teacher's identity and makes calm, reliable behavior an ingrained habit rather than an effortful choice.
quotes: The most important reason is because you made a promise. You said you would follow through every time a class rule was broken. So just for the sake of integrity, it's worth doing.
You see, when you fail to follow your classroom management plan through to the end, you’re telling them that it was all a sham, that you didn’t really mean what you said—not entirely anyway.
For many, their memory of you—the lessons you taught them and the truth and honor you displayed—will keep them afloat through difficult times in their life.
It’s much easier to be consistent when you allow yourself zero wiggle room. Decisions become automatic. Doubt is removed. Stress is all but eliminated.
They’re an opportunity to make the right choice and become not just another teacher . . . But a leader whose example stays with students for the rest of their lives.
